valuation.net_debt_note: EV = market cap + latest borrowings. Screener's public page does not split cash out of other assets, so cash is not netted off; investments are shown separately.

dcf.method: 5-year FCFF: EBITDA - tax on EBIT - capex - change in net working capital; growth fades linearly from the starting rate to the year-5 rate; Gordon terminal value; equity = EV - borrowings.

inputs.growth_basis: median of 3-year, 5-year and TTM sales growth, capped 0-30%
inputs.capex_rule: depreciation + new sales / fixed-asset turnover (median of the last three years)

reverse_dcf.note: Constant sales growth for five years, at the base margin and the same WACC and terminal growth, that makes the DCF equal today's EV.

blocks.text: [F] Accord Transformer & Switchgear Ltd (ATSL) designs, manufactures, supplies, installs and commissions transformers, package/compact substations, switchgear and control panels, busducts and EV-charging power-supply equipment (AR2026 p.38). [F] The revenue engine is oil-cooled and dry-type transformers: in FY26 transformers were 82.7% of revenue, compact and package substations (CSS/PSS) 11.3%, panels 1.2%, services 1.8% and raw-material and other sales 3% (AR2026 p.63). [MC] The CFO put transformers at about Rs 58 crore and PSS/CSS at Rs 8 crore of FY26 revenue (CALL Jun 2026). [F] Revenue is order-based: the company works off customer purchase orders that set specifications, delivery schedules, inspection and warranty terms, and it books revenue on dispatch after the customer clears inspection (AR2026 p.67).

[F] FY26 revenue was Rs 70.05 crore, down from Rs 79.02 crore in FY25, with EBITDA of Rs 7.00 crore (9.99% margin) and PAT of Rs 4.50 crore (NUMBERS). [F] All manufacturing is at two units in the RIICO Industrial Area, Khuskhera, Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, and the head office is in IMT Manesar, Haryana (PPT Jun 2026). [F] The customers named across the documents are power utilities and discoms, renewable-energy EPC contractors, industrial companies and EV-charging infrastructure (AR2026 p.15; CALL Jun 2026). [F] The company does not disclose a revenue split by end market or by customer type. Only the product split above is disclosed (AR2026 p.63).

[F] Geography split: the annual report shows foreign-exchange earnings of nil in both FY25 and FY26 (AR2026 p.55), so on the company's own statutory disclosure FY26 revenue was in effect all domestic. [MC] Marketing material claims a presence across the Middle East, USA, Africa and Asia and more than 1,000 customers served (AR2026 p.6; PPT Jun 2026). [AI] We treat the overseas presence as unquantified and probably immaterial.

Listing status: [F] ATSL listed on the BSE SME platform on 2 March 2026 at an issue price of Rs 46, after a fresh issue of 55,62,000 shares that raised Rs 25.59 crore (AR2026 p.38). [F] The company has published one annual report and one earnings call as a listed entity, reports half-yearly rather than quarterly, and follows Indian GAAP rather than Ind-AS under the SME exemption (AR2026 p.45). [F] The prospectus dated 26 February 2026 was not available to us (AR2026 p.32), so pre-FY24 customer, order and capacity history cannot be checked. [AI] The evidence base is thin, and much of the forward narrative rests on unverified management statements.

subsections.title: Bear thesis: reasons not to own it

items: 1. Valuation is far ahead of any modelled outcome. [F] At Rs 95.9 the stock trades above the bull-case DCF value of Rs 45.2 per share, against a base of Rs 25.6 and a bear of Rs 5.5. The reverse DCF implies 60.7% sales CAGR for five years, against a 17.5% base-case equivalent (NUMBERS).

2. Cash conversion is poor. [F] Cumulative CFO over FY24-FY26 was -0.36x reported PAT, and FCF was -Rs 10.9 cr over the same three years (NUMBERS). [F] FY26 CFO of Rs 8.70 cr depended on a Rs 13.49 cr fall in receivables, partly offset by a Rs 9.09 cr rise in loans and advances (AR2026 p.79).

3. Working capital is heavy and rising. [F] Inventory days rose to 179 and the cash conversion cycle was 121 days in FY26 (NUMBERS). [F] Vendor advances jumped from Rs 0.31 cr to Rs 6.24 cr and stock in transit of Rs 6.20 cr appeared (AR2026 p.89-90).

4. Supplier stretch is concentrated in MSMEs. [F] Rs 14.95 cr of the Rs 18.57 cr of trade payables were owed to micro and small enterprises at Mar 2026, with interest on delayed MSME payments accrued (AR2026 p.87-88). [AI] This is a regulatory and supplier-relationship risk, and payables are a funding source the company may have to unwind.

5. Disclosures contradict each other. [F] Installed capacity is given as 1,200+ MVA (AR2026 p.6) and as 900.36 MVA per annum (PPT Jun 2026). Debt/equity for FY25 is 0.55 (AR2026 p.95) and 0.81 (PPT Jun 2026). Note 2.11(b) says there are no borrowings secured on current assets (AR2026 p.84), while CARO says working-capital limits above Rs 5 cr are sanctioned against current assets (AR2026 p.72).

6. IPO proceeds were re-purposed within six months of listing. [F] None of the Rs 13.03 cr earmarked for machinery had been spent by 2 September 2026, and the board proposed moving Rs 7.00 cr of it to building construction at a new site (AR2026 p.32-33).

7. Customer concentration is high and lumpy. [MC] Torrent Power was about 35-40% of FY25 revenue, and six or seven customers made up about 45% of FY26 revenue (CALL Jun 2026). [MC] A single Rs 31 cr order from one EPC customer, about 44% of FY26 revenue, slipped because of that customer's dispute with the Maharashtra government (CALL Jun 2026).

8. Margins are thin and exposed to commodities. [F] Raw materials consumed were Rs 49.31 cr, about 70% of FY26 revenue (AR2026 p.78). [E] A 10% rise in material cost that could not be passed through would remove about 70% of FY26 EBITDA.

9. Governance infrastructure is immature. [F] The internal auditor is the company's Finance Head, who was CFO from June 2025 until he resigned in January 2026 (AR2026 p.45, p.40). [F] The MD sits on the audit committee (AR2026 p.42). [F] An independent director is a former Vice President at Torrent Power, the largest FY25 customer (PPT Jun 2026).

10. The headline growth narrative rests on an unverified LOI. [MC] The MD described Rs 1,600 cr of compact-substation demand for an NHEV highway EV programme, with 'only our brand approved' and an LOI already issued (CALL Jun 2026). [F] No such LOI or order appears in the exchange announcements available to us (ANNOUNCEMENTS).

blocks.text: [AI] The market appears to be capitalising ATSL's FY27 recovery (revenue +90% in H1 FY27, order book Rs 173 cr) and the transformer-sector narrative as if they will compound for years. Our variant view is that the recovery is largely the release of deferred FY26 orders into FY27, flattering the growth rate. The company's track record of turning profit into cash is negative over three years (NUMBERS). At Rs 95.9, the price sits more than twice the bull-case DCF value (NUMBERS). The underappreciated positive is the post-IPO balance sheet: cash of Rs 22.33 cr against borrowings of Rs 8.36 cr at Mar 2026 (AR2026 p.77, p.87) gives the business room to execute its order book without dilution. The underappreciated negative is disclosure quality. Capacity, ratios, security for borrowings and the shareholding table all contain internal contradictions (AR2026 p.72, p.84, p.85; PPT Jun 2026). For a business whose value rests on management claims, this matters more than usual.

blocks.text: [AI] The listed entity is standalone. The promoter-linked entities sit outside it, and their financials, business scope and any overlap with ATSL's product lines are not disclosed. Whether a non-compete or common-pursuit undertaking exists cannot be checked without the prospectus.

[F] Revenue was only Rs 18.38 cr in FY21 and Rs 48.54 cr in FY24 before reaching Rs 79.02 cr in FY25 (NUMBERS). [AI] The business at today's scale is about two years old. FY25 was the first year above Rs 50 cr and the first with double-digit EBITDA margin (11.6%, NUMBERS). Nearly all of the governance architecture was installed in the 12 months before the IPO: independent directors, CFO, company secretary, committees, statutory auditor rotation, the bonus issue and authorised capital (AR2026 p.39-40, p.44). Investors are underwriting a company with roughly one year of listed-company history, a CFO in post since January 2026, and margins at the current level for only two years.

items: 1. Order capture: [F] customer purchase orders specify technical specs, scope, delivery, inspection, payment and warranty terms (AR2026 p.67). [MC] Utility and long-dated orders carry IEEMA price-variation clauses; orders delivered within about 3 months are fixed-price (CALL Jun 2026).
2. Design and engineering: [MC] in-house design team; R&D described as fully supportive (CALL Jun 2026). [F] R&D expenditure is reported as NIL (AR2026 p.55).

3. Procurement: [MC] copper and CRGO bought against specific orders, about 1 month of stock; oil 1-1.5 months; 3-month price locks with 15% advances to vendors (CALL Jun 2026). [F] Vendor advances were Rs 6.24 cr at Mar 2026 (AR2026 p.90).
4. Core and coil manufacture: [MC] PLC/drive-based winding machines, foil winding, core assembly (PPT Jun 2026; CALL Jun 2026).

5. Tank and sheet-metal fabrication: [MC] plasma cutting, MIG/arc welding, shot blasting and painting (PPT Jun 2026). [MC] Complete sheet-metal and powder-coating capability is planned for the new plant, which implies it is not fully in-house today (CALL Jun 2026).
6. Assembly, oil filling and testing: [MC] automated routine testing in-house (CALL Jun 2026). [F] Type tests such as the dynamic short-circuit test are done at CPRI (AR2026 p.14).

7. Customer inspection and dispatch clearance: [F] revenue is recognised only after inspection clearance and dispatch (AR2026 p.67). [MC] This is why site delays at customers deferred FY26 revenue (CALL Jun 2026).

8. Logistics, installation and service: [MC] third-party logistics with order-wise freight (PPT Jun 2026). [F] Services revenue was Rs 1.24 cr in FY26 (AR2026 p.90). Warranty is backed by bank guarantees of Rs 5.32 cr (AR2026 p.83).

blocks.text: [MC] The MD's own account is that 'product cost almost are same for all manufacturers. Only the margin is different and overheads are different', and that ATSL wins by having lower overheads than larger rivals who outsource to OEMs (CALL Jun 2026). [AI] On this description, value is captured in conversion (winding, assembly, testing) and in qualification (approvals and type tests), not in proprietary technology. [E] The gross margin proxy (revenue less materials consumed and inventory change) rose from 18.9% in FY24 to 23.6% in FY25 and 29.2% in FY26 (AR2026 p.78; PPT Jun 2026). Rising employee and other costs absorbed the gain, so EBITDA margin fell from 11.6% to 9.99% (NUMBERS). [MC] The MD's statement that 'we manufacturing 100% in-house' (CALL Jun 2026) is contradicted by the doubling of job-work expense (AR2026 p.91) and by the plan to bring sheet metal and powder coating in-house (CALL Jun 2026).

[F] Net fixed assets were only Rs 7.95 cr against FY26 revenue of Rs 70.05 cr, a fixed-asset turnover of 8.8x (NUMBERS). [F] Rent of Rs 0.79 cr a year is paid on premises whose ownership and lease terms are not disclosed (AR2026 p.92). [AI] The model is light on fixed assets but heavy on working capital. Net working capital (inventory, receivables, advances and retention money less payables and customer advances) is several times net fixed assets. [F] The planned land (Rs 10.67 cr, ANNOUNCEMENTS) and construction (Rs 7.00 cr, AR2026 p.32) together exceed the entire current net block, so capital intensity is about to step up.

blocks.text: [AI] Standard distribution transformers, panels and busducts are commodity-like: specs are set by the buyer, procurement is by quotation or tender, and the MD concedes 'we have price concern' against lower-category manufacturers (CALL Jun 2026). The more differentiated lines are inverter-duty transformers backed by a CPRI short-circuit test on a 17.6 MVA unit (AR2026 p.14), dry-type transformers and custom CSS/skid packages. These earn on qualification and customisation rather than on IP. [F] No product-level revenue or margin is disclosed beyond the FY26 percentage split (AR2026 p.63), so whether the mix is shifting toward differentiated lines cannot be tested.
[F] FY24 and FY25 product mix is not disclosed (AR2026; PPT Jun 2026). We therefore cannot show a three-year product trend, and say so plainly. [F] The FY24 total was Rs 48.54 cr (NUMBERS).

[F] A 'segment result' is disclosed: manufacturing Rs 3.36 cr and services Rs 1.14 cr in FY26, and Rs 3.66 cr and Rs 2.28 cr in FY25. The two results sum exactly to PAT (AR2026 p.83). [F] The FY25 service-segment result of Rs 2.28 cr exceeds that segment's total revenue of Rs 1.31 cr (AR2026 p.83). [AI] A segment cannot earn more than its revenue, so the allocation is arbitrary and the segment margins are not informative. All assets and liabilities are allocated to manufacturing (AR2026 p.83).

items: [MC] Manufacturing fell because two renewable EPC customers delayed sites: a Rs 31 cr order (25 of 35 transformers built, about Rs 21-22 cr) and a Rs 3 cr order, both due by March 2026 (CALL Jun 2026).
[MC] Transformer-oil availability also curtailed output (CALL Jun 2026).

[AI] Our read: the deferral explanation is plausible and consistent with H1 FY27 revenue of Rs 52.68 cr (ANNOUNCEMENTS). But the FY26 inventory build does not obviously hold Rs 21-22 cr of finished transformers at sales value: finished goods were Rs 3.29 cr and WIP Rs 8.21 cr (AR2026 p.89). The goods may have been in WIP or stock in transit (Rs 6.20 cr), or partly unstarted. This is not reconciled.
[AI] Services were flat at about Rs 1.2 cr and are immaterial.

blocks.text: [AI] Order-driven vs organic: practically all manufacturing revenue is order-driven. Large EPC and utility orders create quarter-to-quarter lumpiness. The small residual of panels, busducts and services behaves more like run-rate business, but it is under 5% of revenue.

subsections.title: Case studies, contracts and the real trend

items: [MC] Disclosed case study: NHEV pilot corridors, where ATSL claims to have supplied transformers and switchgear and supported '20+ CPOs' (PPT Jun 2026). No revenue is attributed to it.

[F] Contract form: customer purchase orders with delivery, inspection and warranty terms (AR2026 p.67). [F] No long-term supply agreements or framework contracts are disclosed. Vendor registrations such as UGVCL's five-year approval confer eligibility, not volume (AR2026 p.14).

[AI] Is concentration improving? Measured by revenue share, possibly: management says the top six or seven made about 45% in FY26 against a single customer at 35-40% in FY25. Measured by risk, no. FY26 revenue fell because one customer's order slipped, and H1 FY27 growth depends on that same order being released. Concentration has moved from one discom customer to a few lumpy EPC orders.

blocks.text: [AI] The client base mixes one meaningful private discom relationship (Torrent), project-based renewable EPC and BESS customers, and a long list of approvals that have not yet produced disclosed revenue. Stickiness is low because nearly all business is won by quotation or tender, which the MD himself describes as needing 'two to three quotations' (CALL Jun 2026). items: Upside: [AI] The base DCF's FY27 sales of Rs 87.7 cr (NUMBERS) look too low given H1 FY27. If H2 FY27 resembles H2 FY25, the bull-case path becomes the floor for FY27. Margin upside from operating leverage is real if the fixed-cost step-up in FY26 does not repeat.

Downside: [AI] Much of H1 FY27 is FY26's deferred revenue. The new plant arrives no earlier than mid-2027, with funding not fully identified. Working capital at about 30% of revenue means faster growth consumes more cash, not less.

[AI] At one end, ATSL executes the new plant, converts utility approvals into tender wins and lands a material NHEV share. Revenue could then exceed the bull case's FY31 Rs 211.7 cr (NUMBERS) with low-teens margins, and the company could graduate to the main board. At the other end, it remains a Rs 80-120 cr regional distribution-transformer supplier with 6-10% margins, lumpy EPC exposure and recurring working-capital strain, closer to the bear-to-base range of Rs 100.7-156.9 cr of FY31 sales (NUMBERS). The documents support the middle of this range far better than the top.

[F] At Rs 95.9, the share price sits above all three DCF values: bear Rs 5.5, base Rs 25.6, bull Rs 45.2 (NUMBERS). [AI] The gap reflects the market capitalising a sharp FY27 recovery, sector enthusiasm and management's narrative (NHEV, EHV, 13-15% margins). Our model does not capitalise any of these, and the documents do not yet evidence them. The operating recovery appears real. What remains unproven is cash conversion, disclosure reliability and the durability of growth beyond the deferred-order release. This is a stock where the evidence base, not the business direction, is the main constraint.

[AI] Investment horizon: any holder is underwriting a two-to-three-year execution story, including the new plant, tender conversion and margin expansion, at a price that already assumes success. Re-review triggers: (1) full H1 FY27 results, expected about November 2026 (margin, CFO, inventory, MSME payables); (2) tender and NHEV order disclosures; (3) FY27 audited results and annual report, around May-September 2027 (guidance test, auditor remarks, capacity and order-book disclosure); (4) any further IPO-object variation, CFO change or auditor change.

[F] This is our initial coverage of Accord Transformer & Switchgear Ltd; no prior report exists for comparison. The guidance tracker in this report (FY27 revenue Rs 120-180 cr, EBITDA margin 13-15%, PAT margin 9-11%, new-plant timing, NHEV stations, tender outcomes) sets the baseline for testing at the next review (CALL Jun 2026).

summary.one_line: Accord Transformer's FY27 revenue rebound and Rs 173 cr order book look real, but at Rs 95.9 the stock trades above even the bull-case DCF value of Rs 45.2 and needs about 61% sales CAGR for five years, while three-year cash conversion is negative and disclosures contradict one another.
